extracted.intended_audience: children's and YA authors, researchers of children's literature, educators, and publishers concerned with disability representation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and ethically representing disabled characters in children's and young adult fiction, and parallel considerations for researchers who represent disabled participants. Emphasises authenticity, research, accessibility and minimizing harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical responsibility to create well-rounded, accurate and authentic disabled characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors have an important ethical responsibility when including disability in their writing to create well‑rounded, accurate and authentic disabled characters, similar to the ethical responsibility researchers have to authentically represent participants and their experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues that because children's books reach wide audiences, incorrect and stereotypical representations can cause real harm. Authors should take this responsibility seriously to improve representations read by children and teenagers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity: accuracy complemented by personality not defined by disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity is defined (via the 'Reading the Way' report) as 'whereby accuracy is complemented by a personality that is not defined by disability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure accuracy of lived experience while making the character's personality distinct from, and not reduced to, their disability. Use authenticity as both factual accuracy and dimensional characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotypical portrayals that present disability as pity or deficit
rubrics_metrics.description: Problematic representations portray disabled characters as objects of pity who have a deficit, which can do real harm to disabled people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make disability the source of pity or the only lens through which a character is presented. Be alert to tropes that infantilize, heroify, or pity disabled characters; consider how such portrayals shape readers' attitudes and disable readers' sense of self.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make disability part of the character, not the sole focus driving the narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Disability can be one aspect of a character and not the focus of the story; it should not be what drives the narrative or wholly define the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in She Is Not Invisible Laureth's blindness is one aspect of her character and the story is driven by her quest to find her father. Authors might consider not revealing or foregrounding disability in a way that reduces the character to a condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict lived experience concretely: sensory perspective and environmental barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect the complex realities of lived experience (e.g., using senses other than sight for a blind character) and include environmental barriers and accommodations that affect daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative techniques (sensory detail, perspective) to give readers insight into how a character experiences the world; show structural barriers (e.g., inaccessible environments) and accommodations (e.g., tactile currency) to increase realism and empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct meticulous research and consult people with lived experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should research and engage directly with people who have the disability being represented (e.g., Sedgwick's visits to New College Worcester and long conversations with blind and visually impaired students).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First‑hand research and sustained contact with community members strengthens authenticity. Treat consultation as substantive (not tokenistic) and be transparent about sources of knowledge. Recognize limits: one person's experience is not universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect ownvoices concerns; take extra care when not writing from ownvoices
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author is not writing from an ownvoices perspective, they carry additional ethical responsibility to respect experiences and views of people with that disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not writing ownvoices, seek meaningful engagement with people with lived experience, include their perspectives in development/review, and avoid claiming that a single portrayal represents all experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accessible dissemination (publish in multiple accessible formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors/publishers should consider how the book is disseminated and make it available in accessible formats (hardback, eBook, audiobook, large print, Braille, DAISY etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simultaneous publication in accessible formats demonstrates respect for disabled readers and improves equitable access to literature. Plan accessibility at publication rather than as an afterthought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating disability as homogenous or universally representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Disability is not a homogenous experience and a portrayal should not be presented as representative of all people with that condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge diversity within disability communities; avoid generalizing from one character's traits or experiences to all disabled people. Use varied characters or contextualize the limits of a portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of and minimize the impact of representations on readers' attitudes and potential harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Representations of disability can affect non‑disabled young readers' views of disabled people and can reflect disabled readers' lived experiences back to them, with potential for harm if inaccurate or stereotypical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider downstream effects: how portrayals shape attitudes, expectations, stigma, or self‑perception. Use sensitivity reading, community feedback, and reflective practice to reduce harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include diverse attitudes toward disability within the story world
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent varying attitudes encountered by disabled people (acceptance, ignorance, rudeness etc.) to show social realities and nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict a range of reactions from other characters (e.g., automatic acceptance vs. institutional ignorance) to avoid one‑dimensional social responses and to reflect lived social complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice ethical reflexivity and cross-disciplinary learning in research and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers and researchers should reflect on their own positionality and seek solutions and connections across academic and disciplinary boundaries when representing disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use insights from empirical research, education, disability studies and community engagement to inform representation; be reflexive about the ethical implications of depiction and research practices.
